title: The vineyard tenants (Mark 12:1–12)
hook: the stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone

segments.voice: Yesterday, a trap in the temple courts, and your line was answer with a question. Did you hand one good question back? Day two hundred ten. The end of the week.

Still in the temple courts, with the leaders still listening, Jesus tells a story. A man plants a vineyard. He builds a hedge around it, digs a winepress, puts up a watchtower. Anyone who knew their scriptures would hear Isaiah, whose song pictured Israel as God's vineyard. Then the owner rents it to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share. They beat him and send him off empty. He sends another; they hit him on the head. Another; they kill him. Many more, beaten or killed. He has one left: his son, his beloved. Surely they'll respect my son. And the tenants look at each other. This is the heir. Kill him, and it's all ours.
screen: `A VINEYARD, A HEDGE, A TOWER.` → `SERVANT AFTER SERVANT.` → `LAST OF ALL, THE BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: They kill him and throw him out of the vineyard. What will the owner do? He'll come and put an end to those tenants and give the vineyard to others. Then Jesus quotes a psalm, in the King James Bible: "The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner." Picture builders sorting stones, tossing one onto the rubbish heap as useless. Later, that very stone turns out to be the one holding the corners of the whole building together. It's from Psalm 118, the same psalm the crowds had sung days earlier: blessed is he that cometh. Many readers point out a wordplay in Hebrew, where son is ben and stone is even. The son they reject becomes the stone everything rests on. Christians hear the whole story of Jesus in it: sent last, beloved, rejected, killed, and made the cornerstone. Mark says the leaders understood he'd told it against them, and wanted to arrest him, but feared the crowd, so they left. It's important to read that carefully. This parable has sometimes been misused to claim God rejected the Jewish people. Mark himself points it at a handful of leaders, while the crowd, Jewish too, stands with Jesus. Many churches today say plainly that the anti-Jewish reading is wrong. Now look back at the week. Ransom, and not to be served but to serve. Bartimaeus asked what do you want. A borrowed colt. A fig tree and a temple. Faith that moves mountains, and forgive, then pray. A question answered with a question. And the rejected stone. All week, the road has been leading to one place, and the stone is part of what's waiting there.
screen: `THEY THROW THE SON OUT.` · `THE REJECTED STONE.` · `BEN AND EVEN: SON AND STONE.` · `AIMED AT A FEW, NOT A PEOPLE.` · then, large: `THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED IS BECOME THE HEAD OF THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the stone someone threw aside. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person others tend to overlook. The quiet kid. The colleague whose ideas get talked over. The neighbor nobody visits. Someone the builders tossed on the pile. Picture them. What do they hold up that nobody notices? What would it look like to value them out loud? If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The vineyard tenants. A story of servants rejected and a beloved son killed, and a rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone.
Your line: the rejected stone. Today, tell one overlooked person specifically what they do that matters. Day two hundred ten.

howItsDone: Christians often call Jesus the cornerstone, drawing on this psalm, and many churches mark the laying of a building's cornerstone with a service; many churches today also teach explicitly against reading this parable as a rejection of the Jewish people.

original.note: Hebrew: stone, in Psalm 118:22. many hear a wordplay with ben, son.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bad renters.
what it means: servants and a beloved son rejected, and the rejected one becomes the cornerstone.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 5's vineyard, Psalm 118:22, and a likely Hebrew pun between ben and even, son and stone.

notes: Sensitive: the script explicitly rejects the supersessionist/anti-Jewish reading and notes Mark points the parable at the leaders (12:12). Keeper to confirm tone and accuracy for all churches.
ben/even wordplay is a common suggestion (possibly behind the use of Psalm 118 here); stated as 'many readers point out'.
